green.title: City of Toronto · Green Bin guide

apartments.title: City of Toronto · Apartment collection support

stats.scope: City-serviced residential waste; diversion includes recycling and other diverted materials. Blue Bin tonnes include estimates. These figures do not measure composting participation or explain the causes of the gap.

items.name: Banana peel
items.action: Remove stickers and separate any packaging. Put the peel in your building’s organics bin or your household Green Bin.

items.name: Vegetable scraps
items.action: Separate packaging and produce stickers. Vegetable scraps belong in the Green Bin.

items.name: Fruit cores
items.action: Fruit cores and pits belong in the Green Bin. Remove any stickers or packaging.

items.name: Fruit peels
items.action: Fruit peels belong in the Green Bin. Remove produce stickers first.

items.name: Avocado peel & pit
items.action: The skin and pit can go in the Green Bin, even though a pit breaks down slowly in a small home composter.

items.name: Coffee grounds
items.action: Coffee grounds and paper filters belong in the Green Bin. Coffee pods are a different item: check Waste Wizard.

items.name: Paper tea bag
items.action: Paper tea bags can go in the Green Bin. For nylon or silk bags, empty the tea into organics and put the bag in garbage.

items.name: Eggshells
items.action: Eggshells belong in the Green Bin. An egg carton is a separate item.

items.name: Mixed food scraps
items.action: Separate all packaging. Food scraps, including cooked food, can go in Toronto’s Green Bin. Keep meat, dairy and oily food out of the Calmpost compost bin.

items.name: Meat scraps
items.action: Keep meat out of your small Calmpost compost bin. Toronto’s Green Bin accepts meat; remove all packaging first.

items.name: Fish
items.action: Keep fish out of your small compost bin. Toronto’s Green Bin accepts fish and shellfish, including bones and shells.

items.name: Chicken & meat bones
items.action: Keep bones out of your small compost bin. Toronto’s Green Bin accepts meat and fish bones.

items.name: Cheese & dairy
items.action: Keep dairy out of your small compost bin. Remove packaging and place the food in Toronto’s Green Bin.

items.name: Bread
items.action: Toronto’s Green Bin accepts bread and baked goods. Calmpost keeps bread out of its small compost bin to limit pests.

items.name: Oily food leftovers
items.action: Food leftovers belong in the Green Bin after removing packaging. This advice is for food, not a container of liquid cooking oil. Check Waste Wizard for oil disposal.

items.name: Paper towel
items.action: Food-soiled paper towels can go in the Green Bin. If soiled with cleaning chemicals, use garbage instead.

items.name: Food-soiled pizza box
items.action: Remove plastic pieces. Food-soiled, uncoated pizza cardboard can go in the Green Bin; clean cardboard is recycled.

items.name: Compostable plastic cutlery
items.action: A compostable label does not make plastic cutlery suitable for Toronto’s Green Bin. Put it in garbage. Choose reusable cutlery next time.

items.name: Compostable plastic coffee cup
items.action: Cups made of or lined with compostable plastic are not accepted in Toronto’s Green Bin. Put them in garbage; bring a reusable cup next time.

items.name: Clean paper egg carton
items.action: Empty, clean paper egg cartons belong in residential recycling. Food-soiled paper cartons can go in the Green Bin. Foam and plastic cartons are different items.

items.name: Clean newspaper
items.action: Clean newspaper belongs in residential recycling. Separate any plastic wrap and remove elastic bands.

items.name: Clean unwaxed cardboard
items.action: Clean, unwaxed cardboard belongs in recycling. Flatten it and follow your building’s set-out instructions. Food-soiled, uncoated cardboard can go in organics.

items.name: Dry leaves
items.action: Leave fallen leaves where practical, or use your yard waste service. Leaves are separate from kitchen organics; ask building management about your building’s arrangements.

items.name: Grass clippings
items.action: Leave clippings on your lawn or use an outdoor composter. Toronto does not collect grass clippings in yard waste, Green Bin or garbage.
